PEGylation of nanoparticles reduces uptake by mononuclear phagocyte system cells, increasing circulation time up to 45 hours in humans.
Tumor blood vessels have pore sizes ranging from 100 nm to 1 µm, enabling nanoparticle extravasation via the EPR effect.
Stealth nanoparticles are typically designed to be smaller than 200 nm with neutral and hydrophilic surfaces.
Doxil® (PEGylated liposomal doxorubicin) was the first stealth nanocarrier approved by the FDA and EMA for cancer therapy.
Doxil® increases plasma AUC of doxorubicin approximately 300-fold in humans compared to free drug.
Paclitaxel formulations like Taxol® use Cremophor EL®, which causes hypersensitivity reactions mitigated by premedication.
Genexol-PM is a Cremophor-free, PEG–PLA micellar formulation of paclitaxel approved in South Korea with improved toxicity profile.
Active targeting ligands grafted on PEGylated nanoparticles include anti-HER2 antibodies, RGD peptides, and folate.
PEGylated nanoparticles show decreased aggregation and opsonization due to steric stabilization by PEG chains.
The impaired lymphatic drainage in tumors contributes to nanoparticle retention after extravasation.
Surface modification with PEG or polysaccharides provides steric repulsion that prevents protein adsorption and immune recognition.
Clinical trials have demonstrated improved therapeutic efficacy and reduced systemic toxicity with stealth nanocarriers.
The mononuclear phagocyte system primarily clears nanoparticles via recognition of opsonized proteins on their surface.
Liposomes, polymeric nanoparticles, micelles, solid lipid nanoparticles, and lipid nanocapsules are common stealth nanocarrier types.
Active targeting can increase cellular uptake and tumor penetration beyond passive accumulation.
PEG molecular weight, density, and conformation on the nanoparticle surface critically influence stealth properties.
Stealth nanoparticles can carry hydrophobic drugs like paclitaxel and docetaxel, improving their solubility and delivery.
The EPR effect is dependent on tumor type, size, and vascular architecture, influencing nanoparticle accumulation.
Stealth nanocarriers have been developed to deliver not only chemotherapeutics but also proteins, DNA, and siRNA.
The first generation of nanoparticles had short circulation half-lives due to rapid opsonization and clearance.
PEGylation was first applied to liposomes in the late 1980s to create long-circulating stealth nanoparticles.
